newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak rates fall as central bank injects liquidity.
newsitem.headline: Slovak rates fall as central bank injects liquidity.

text.p: Slovak interbank interest rates fell sharply on Monday after the central bank signalled it would continue to add market liquidity, though dealers said the market remained volatile.
The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) added 6.0 billion crowns through a one-week repo tender on Monday, pushing down the average yield to 17.25 percent from 18.78 percent on Friday.
Interbank rates with maturities of up to one month followed suit, easing to around 22 percent after opening at around 30 percent.

Traders said the NBS repo signalled the central bank intended to continue adding crown liquidity, which should help it overcome a severe liquidity crunch after several weeks of uncertainty caused by an attack on the crown in May and June.

But they added the market in general was still tense. "The market will remain fragile as the banking sector will continue to depend on NBS repo tenders for some time," said Jaroslav Hora, chief money market dealer at VUB Bank.
"This means the central bank will be able to squeeze crown liquidity easily within a short period of time if it wishes to do so," Hora added.
Traders said rates were unlikely to decline further and doubted they would fall below the 20 percent level.
The NBS restricted market liquidity to support the crown during the crisis in an attempt to make speculative purchases of hard currencies expensive.
The strategy appears to have worked as the crown is now stable, between its mark/dollar basket parity and one percent on the basket's weak side.
But the central bank moves also paralysed trading on the interbank market, which has yet to recover fully and where daily volumes are now only about half of those before the run on the currency.
"The volume and rates in the NBS repo calmed the market and interbank rates moved downward," said Martin Hrozany of Credit Lyonnais bank.
Local banks are expected to meet their minimum reserve requirements on Tuesday, having failed to do so four times in succession over the past two months.
"The sector will probably meet its PMR, but it depends on borrowed money and we can only expect higher liquidity after larger amounts of state securities mature in the next two months," Hrozany said.
Some 6.8 billion crowns in treasury bills are due to mature by the end of July and additional funds from T-bills worth 9.3 billion crowns will return to the interbank market in August.
